title: Sansara

teacherSummary.text: Over many years Siddhartha grows wealthy, gambles, drinks, and becomes greedy and weary—like the childlike people. Kamala tells him she wishes to learn about Gotama. After a dream of Kamala's songbird lying dead in its golden cage, Siddhartha feels disgust at his life and leaves the city without a word. Kamala, pregnant with his child, frees her bird.

vocabulary.definition: To play or game for money or other stake
vocabulary.context: Thus he gambled with high stakes and mercilessly, hating himself, mocking himself, won thousands, threw away thousands, lost money, lost jewelry, lost a house in the country, won again, lost again.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “gamble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: One who, or that which, is cast away or shipwrecked
vocabulary.context: Alone he stood there and empty like a castaway on the shore.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “castaway”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: And after each big loss, his mind was set on new riches, pursued the trade more zealously, forced his debtors more strictly to pay, because he wanted to continue gambling, he wanted to continue squandering, continue demonstrating his disdain of wealth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “demonstrate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: He played the game due to a pain of his heart, losing and wasting his wretched money in the game brought him an angry joy, in no other way he could demonstrate his disdain for wealth, the merchants’ false god, more clearly and more mockingly.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “mockingly”: -ly (Old English -lice, "in the manner of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: On a strange and devious way, Siddhartha had gotten into this final and most base of all dependencies, by means of the game of dice.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “devious”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Filled with, or characterized by, zeal
vocabulary.context: And after each big loss, his mind was set on new riches, pursued the trade more zealously, forced his debtors more strictly to pay, because he wanted to continue gambling, he wanted to continue squandering, continue demonstrating his disdain of wealth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “zealous”: -ous (Latin -osus, "full of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: And after each big loss, his mind was set on new riches, pursued the trade more zealously, forced his debtors more strictly to pay, because he wanted to continue gambling, he wanted to continue squandering, continue demonstrating his disdain of wealth.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “debtor”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: Suitable or fit to be relied on
vocabulary.context: He only noticed that this bright and reliable voice inside of him, which had awoken in him at that time and had ever guided him in his best times, had become silent.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “reliable”: re- (Latin re-, "back, again"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To circumscribe or go round so as to surround closely
vocabulary.context: Starting up from this dream, he felt encompassed by a deep sadness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “encompass”: en- (French en-/Latin in-, "into") + pass (Latin passus, "step"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: Domestic fowls reared for the table, or for their eggs or feathers, such as cocks and hens, capons, turkeys, ducks,…
vocabulary.context: He had learned to eat tenderly and carefully prepared food, even fish, even meat and poultry, spices and sweets, and to drink wine, which causes sloth and forgetfulness.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “poultry”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Samsara (spelled 'Sansara' in this translation) is the cycle of birth, suffering and rebirth.

significance: The caged songbird is the book's clearest symbol of Siddhartha's trapped inner voice.
discussionQuestions: What does the dead songbird symbolize?
Where does symbolism appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with experience versus teaching?

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Sansara,” how does Hesse show the cycle of desire? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Sansara, how does Hesse develop the idea of the cycle of desire? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the symbolism in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Sansara develops the idea of the cycle of desire. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of symbolism and theme shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Sansara (where it begins, turns and ends) and its symbolism shape the reader's understanding of the cycle of desire. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Sansara suggests about the cycle of desire. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's symbolism and theme), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses symbolism in Sansara to complicate the reader's understanding of the cycle of desire. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Sansara within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of the cycle of desire responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Sansara alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of the cycle of desire follows or bends those conventions, using the symbolism as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Sansara and its treatment of the cycle of desire. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's symbolism and theme, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Sansara as evidence for a larger claim about the cycle of desire in Siddhartha. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Sansara as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of the cycle of desire. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does the dead songbird symbolize? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are gambled, castaway, demonstrating, mockingly, devious. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Thus he gambled with high stakes and mercilessly, hating himself, mocking himself, won thousands, threw away thousands, lost money, lost jewelry, lost a house in the country, won again, lost again.” Webster's says: To play or game for money or other stake. Now the word history: “gamble”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “castaway”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. “demonstrate”: de- (Latin de, "down from, away") + -ate (Latin -atus, "to make, having"). Root not in our table: have students find it. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Samsara (spelled 'Sansara' in this translation) is the cycle of birth, suffering and rebirth. Why does this chapter matter? The caged songbird is the book's clearest symbol of Siddhartha's trapped inner voice. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for symbolism.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see symbolism, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to the cycle of desire.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Symbolism, Theme, Tone / mood.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of symbolism. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Starting up from this dream, he felt encompassed by a deep sadness. Worthless, so it seemed to him, worthless and pointless was the way he had been going through life; nothing which was alive, nothing which was in some way delicious or worth keeping he had left in his hands. Alone he stood there and empty like a castaway on the shore.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Symbolism, Theme, Tone / mood: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Sansara,” how does Hesse show the cycle of desire? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the symbolism you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about the cycle of desire, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how symbolism shapes the cycle of desire. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
